subtitle: Verbs with unusual frames, and the connectors of formal German
words.intro: It’s said that three Germans in a room will found a club, and then appoint a treasurer. The annual meeting of a club has an agenda, minutes and the audit of the accounts. It’s also the last place in Germany where the genitive is still in everyday use.

grammar[0].fact: The genitive object is on its way out of spoken German, and it won’t be missed in the pub. But it’s holding on in court, in church and at a club’s annual meeting. *Wir gedenken seiner* carries a weight that *Wir denken an ihn* doesn’t.

grammar[1].fact: These words won’t make you sound clever unless your word order is right. *Wiewohl* sends the verb to the end, and *gleichwohl* pulls it forward. And no one has ever used *mithin* at a bus stop, except perhaps a retired judge.

document.intro: A real plaque on a club’s shooting range in Austria, and it’s almost a set of minutes. Notice the passive at the end of each entry: *wird … errichtet*. Notice too how it thanks the Emperor in a phrase: *mit großzügiger Unterstützung*.
document.fact: Ferlach is a real town of gunmakers in Carinthia, with a long tradition of hunting rifles. Three hundred metres is a very long range for a small club, and a *Kleinkaliberhalle* is a hall for small-bore rifles.

reading.title: Tagesordnungspunkt 7
reading.intro: The annual meeting of the Schützenverein 1887. Item 7: the accounts. There are 14 euros and 20 cents missing, and the treasurer, Herr Gruber, has held that post for 31 years. Dr. Brummer is taking the minutes. Max joined two weeks ago, because Lena’s uncle asked him to. He hasn’t yet realised that this is serious.
reading.fact: Germany has over half a million registered clubs, and a registered one, or *e. V.*, needs at least seven founders and a written constitution. The *Schützenverein* began as a citizens’ militia. Today, its annual shooting festival crowns a king, and in many villages it’s the event of the year.
